messages.subject: mirt version 0.9.0 on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Next release has been sent to CRAN and looks to be built for all platforms. Check the NEWS file for a description of the user visible updates and new features, the most annoying and code breaking of which is the removal of the confmirt() and confmirt.model() functions, which have been replaced by a method = 'MHRM' argument in the mirt() function and mirt.model().

Additionally, I've made a neat interactive tool via the 'shiny' package that provides a wrapper to the itemplot() function, which might be useful for understanding how mirt parametrizes various items types, and what happens to other dependent item functions (like expected item lines, information trace lines, etc). You can load the utility after installing the shiny package by using

> shiny::runGist('6337165')

Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
hi phil and my fellow mirt-users,

i have a (maybe more general) question regarding the parametrization of the gpcm-model in mirt.

so far, when i used ltm to estimate my models, the gpcm-parameters were the points on the theta-scale were the probability functions of two adjacent categories met.

how can i transform the gpcm-parameters given by mirt into these?

see below an example with the science-data

library(ltm)
library(mirt)

dat = sapply(Science, as.numeric)[, c(-2,-5:-6)]

ltm_model = gpcm(dat)
mirt_model = mirt(dat, model = 1, itemtype="gpcm")

coef(ltm_model)
coef(mirt_model)

plot(ltm_model, item = 1)
abline(v = coef(ltm_model)[1,1:3]) # the threshold-params as vertical lines

thanks a lot!

messages.subject: Re: gpcm parametrization
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felix,

I've received lots of requests to convert the parametrization I use to
the more traditional metrics, but I just haven't put it high enough on
the priority list to do it (github pull request anyone?). Here's how
to convert the gpcm into what you see in ltm (the slopes should be the
same):

ds <- coef(mirt_model, digits = 10)[[2]][-1]
a <- coef(mirt_model, digits = 10)[[2]][1]

dprime <- ds/a
ltmds <- numeric(3)
for(i in 1:3) ltmds[i] <- -(dprime[i+1]-dprime[i])
ltmds

A similar argument can be used for the nominal model, since they share
similar parametrizations. Hope that helps!

Phil

messages.subject: Re: fitIndices()
messages.body_plain:
No, fitIndicies is used to compute the M2 stat, which requires
numerical integration from known parameters. The estimator to get the
model won't matter, so the problem isn't really related to the MH-RM.

The M2 stat is really computationally intensive, even in
unidimensional models (which this one isn't), and is less than
practical in a number of practical situations since it depends on the
number of first and second moment combinations in the data, which for
even a moderate number of items can become massive. It also depends on
the sample size, since larger sample sizes means more potential
combinations for first and second moments (larger data saturation).

Some research is being done regarding this problem use large sample
approximation approaches, but for now I don't really have a practical
solution....besides maybe splitting the data into smaller chunks and
using the stat that way (Albert Maydeu-Olivares suggested doing this
as well). Sorry for the annoyance.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: standard error in fscores(..., full.scores=TRUE)
messages.body_plain:
Not really, but you could just use some of the code already rolled
from the package like so:

###
library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(Science, 1)
scores <- fscores(mod)
scoremat <- scores[,c('F1', 'SE_F1')]

#verbatim from the package code
tabdata2 <- object@tabdatalong
tabdata2 <- tabdata2[,-ncol(tabdata2)]
stabdata2 <- apply(tabdata2, 1, paste, sep='', collapse = '/')
sfulldata <- apply(object@fulldata, 1, paste, sep='', collapse = '/')
scoremat <- scores[match(sfulldata, stabdata2), , drop = FALSE]
colnames(scoremat) <- colnames(scores)

head(scoremat)
###

Might be better to make a function do this, but I think you get the
idea. That's kind of a weird feature to include by default though, but
I guess if anyone else wants it then I'll consider adding it. Cheers.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: How to fix mean and variance of latent variables with confmirt()?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I would like to know how to fix the mean and variance of the latent variables when specifying a model with confmirt.model().

Cheers, Jens
messages.body_snippet:
Hi,

messages.subject: Re: How to fix mean and variance of latent variables with confmirt()?
messages.subject_clean: How to fix mean and variance of latent variables with confmirt()?
messages.body_plain:
This question was migrated from Cross-Validated, so here's the
background syntax that was proposed:

####

require(mirt)

# Generate the data

a <- matrix(c(1, NA, NA, 1, NA, NA, NA, 1, NA, NA, 1, NA, NA, NA, 1, NA, NA, 1),
            ncol=3, byrow=TRUE)

d <- matrix(c(-1, NA, 1, NA, -1, NA, 1, NA, -1, NA, 1, NA), ncol=2,
byrow = TRUE)
type = c("dich", "dich","dich","dich","dich","dich")

simdat <- simdata(a, d, 100, itemtype = type)

# Specify the model

model1 <- confmirt.model()
1: F1 = 1 - 2
2: F2 = 3 - 4
3: F3 = 5 - 6
4: COV = F1*F2, F1*F3, F2*F3
5: SLOPE = F1@1 eq 1, F1@2 eq 1, F2@3 eq 1, F2@4 eq 1, F3@5 eq 1, F3@6 eq 1

#Fit the model

c_model1 <- confmirt(simdat, model1)

####

Looking at this it appears you are using a much older version of mirt,
and the current version on CRAN is version 0.9.0. The latest doesn't
include the confmirt.model() or confmirt() functions, and instead have
either been renamed (mirt.model()) or can be accessed by a method
argument(confmirt(...) is now the same as mirt(..., method = 'MHRM')).
Also I dropped support for the SLOPE, INT, and PRIOR arguments in the
original article since I found them to be a bit cumbersome and not
very R like. I'd recommend checking out the examples on Github for
getting a feel for the new package layout, and there are a handful of
exercises and examples that have been worked through there.

To get you started after you update to version 0.9.0, you want to edit
the starting values directly, so passing sv <- mirt(data, model, pars
= 'values') will give a data.frame called sv containing all the
starting values and whether they are estimated. Modify this object to
your liking (you can use the sv <- edit(sv) function if you prefer to
use a GUI) and pass this back into the estimation function with
mirt(data, model, pars = sv). Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: about calibratiıng data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Neese,

mirt uses a different parameterization for a and d than the traditional IRT metric that PARSCALE uses.  If you've done everything correctly, the a parameter should match across results from mirt and PARSCALE; but the d will differ.  You can convert the parameters easily by hand by using:

b = - d / a

Further,

z = a(Theta - b) = a Theta + d

So,

d = - a*b

messages.subject: Re: standard error in fscores(..., full.scores=TRUE)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felix,

The prior is usually as you suspect for unidimensional MAP and EAP
scores, N(0,1), or more generally, N ∼ (0, I) in the multivariate
exploratory case. This information comes from how you estimated the
latent covariance parameters, so for confirmatory/multiple group
models I will use the group parameters as indicators of the prior
distribution, while for single group the majority of the time it's the
standardized orthogonal multivariate normal. Use coef(), summary(), or
mod2values() on your object to locate the group parameters.

You can specify your own prior mean and covariances however if you
want something other than the model's 'group' parameters (possibly
something more diffuse). Naturally, making the prior more defuse will
influence the estimates less, and providing a sufficiently
uninformative prior to MAP estimation will give scores identical to ML
estimation (expect that extreme response patterns will still be
estimated and won't actually converge....). I've found this useful
when ML scores don't converge but you still want ML-like estimates, so
providing a poor prior will help to stabilize these response patterns
to obtain reasonable values while still not being overly influential.
Cheers.

Phil
